objectives: Explain occlusion and Angle's Class I, II, and III classification of malocclusion.
Compare fixed and removable prosthodontics and describe dental implants and osseointegration.
Describe the appliances and analytical tools of orthodontics, including brackets, archwires, clear aligners, and cephalometric analysis.

slides.title: Occlusion and Angle's classification of malocclusion
slides.body:
**Occlusion** is the way the teeth of the upper and lower arches meet when the jaws close. Understanding occlusion is the foundation of both **prosthodontics** (replacing teeth) and **orthodontics** (aligning teeth), because every restoration and every tooth movement must fit a functioning bite. In **maximum intercuspation (centric occlusion)** the cusps interdigitate fully; **centric relation** is a reproducible jaw position determined by the temporomandibular joints. Ideal function also requires **anterior guidance** and **canine guidance**, in which the front and canine teeth disclude the back teeth during jaw movement, protecting them from damaging lateral forces.

The single most influential framework for describing the bite is **Angle's classification of malocclusion**, devised by **Edward Hartley Angle (1855–1930)**, the American dentist universally regarded as the **"father of modern orthodontics"** and founder of the first orthodontic school. Published around **1899**, Angle's system uses the **first permanent molars** as the key landmark, specifically the relationship of the upper first molar's **mesiobuccal cusp** to the lower first molar:

- **Class I (neutrocclusion)** — the mesiobuccal cusp of the upper first molar occludes in the buccal groove of the lower first molar; the molar relationship is normal even if individual teeth are crowded or rotated.
- **Class II (distocclusion)** — the lower molar sits **distally (posteriorly)** relative to the upper; the upper teeth are too far forward. Class II is subdivided into **Division 1** (protruding upper incisors, an "overjet") and **Division 2** (retroclined upper central incisors). This is the classic "overbite" profile with a retruded chin.
- **Class III (mesiocclusion)** — the lower molar sits **mesially (anteriorly)** relative to the upper; the lower jaw is prognathic, producing the "underbite" or protruding-lower-jaw profile.

**Malocclusion** — any deviation from ideal occlusion — also includes **overjet** (horizontal overlap of incisors), **overbite** (vertical overlap), **open bite** (front teeth not meeting), **crossbite** (a reversed buccolingual relationship), and **crowding** or **spacing**. Severity is often quantified with indices such as the **Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN)** and the **Peer Assessment Rating (PAR)**. Angle's molar-based scheme, more than a century old, remains the universal shorthand by which clinicians communicate a patient's bite.

slides.title: Prosthodontics — fixed, removable, and implant-supported
slides.body:
**Prosthodontics** is the dental specialty devoted to **restoring and replacing teeth** with artificial substitutes. It divides broadly into fixed and removable approaches, with implants now spanning both.

**Fixed prosthodontics** replaces or restores teeth with prostheses **cemented or bonded permanently** in place. The chief examples are **crowns** (full-coverage restorations of a single tooth) and **fixed partial dentures (bridges)**, in which an artificial tooth (the **pontic**) is suspended between crowned **abutment** teeth on either side of a gap. A **resin-bonded (Maryland) bridge** uses metal or ceramic wings bonded to the backs of adjacent teeth, conserving tooth structure. Fixed work demands precise impressions or digital scans and careful attention to occlusion.

**Removable prosthodontics** provides appliances the patient can take out: **complete dentures** for the edentulous (toothless) arch and **removable partial dentures (RPDs)** that clasp onto remaining teeth. Successful dentures depend on **retention** (resistance to vertical dislodging forces, aided by the suction of the **peripheral seal**), **stability**, and **support** from the underlying ridge and mucosa.

The greatest advance in tooth replacement was the **dental implant**. The Swedish orthopaedic surgeon **Per-Ingvar Brånemark** discovered in the 1950s, while studying bone healing with titanium optical chambers, that **bone bonds intimately to titanium** — a phenomenon he named **osseointegration**, defined as a direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the surface of a load-bearing implant. He placed the first titanium dental implants in a human (**Gösta Larsson**) in **1965**, and the protocol was published internationally in the late 1970s. A modern implant is a **titanium (or titanium-alloy) "root"** surgically placed in the jawbone; after osseointegration over weeks to months, an **abutment** and a **crown, bridge, or denture** are attached. Implant surfaces are roughened (by sandblasting and acid-etching, or with hydroxyapatite or **SLA** treatments) to speed integration. Implants can support a single crown, a bridge, or an entire arch (for example the **"All-on-4"** concept). The chief biological complication is **peri-implantitis**, an inflammatory loss of supporting bone analogous to periodontitis, underscoring that even titanium teeth require meticulous hygiene and maintenance.

slides.title: Orthodontics — appliances, biomechanics, and cephalometrics
slides.body:
**Orthodontics** moves teeth and guides jaw growth to correct malocclusion. Tooth movement is fundamentally a **biological** process: a controlled force applied to a tooth creates **pressure and tension zones** in the periodontal ligament, recruiting **osteoclasts** to resorb bone on the pressure side and **osteoblasts** to deposit bone on the tension side, so the tooth migrates through the alveolus. **Light, continuous forces** are most efficient and least damaging; excessive force causes **hyalinisation** and root resorption.

The classic appliance is the **fixed appliance**, or **braces**, refined from Angle's original "edgewise" appliance. Its components are:
- **Brackets** — small attachments bonded to each tooth (metal, ceramic, or self-ligating designs) that hold the wire.
- **Archwires** — wires that thread through the brackets and deliver the force. Treatment typically begins with flexible **nickel–titanium (NiTi)** wires that exploit **superelasticity** to align crowded teeth gently, then progresses to stiffer **stainless-steel** or **beta-titanium (TMA)** wires for precise positioning and space closure.
- **Auxiliaries** — elastics (rubber bands), springs, and at times **temporary anchorage devices (TADs/mini-screws)** that provide skeletal anchorage. A landmark refinement was the **straight-wire appliance** introduced by **Lawrence Andrews** in the 1970s, which built tooth-specific prescriptions into the brackets; Andrews also defined the **"six keys to normal occlusion."**

A major modern alternative is the **clear aligner**, a series of removable, transparent thermoplastic trays that incrementally move the teeth. **Invisalign**, launched by **Align Technology** in **1998** (founders **Zia Chishti** and **Kelsey Wirth**), made this approach mainstream; aligners are now planned with digital scans and 3D-printed models. **Functional appliances** (such as the **Twin Block** and **Herbst**) harness growth to correct skeletal Class II problems in children.

Diagnosis and treatment planning rely on **cephalometric analysis** — the measurement of standardised lateral skull radiographs (**cephalograms**), introduced for orthodontics by **B. Holly Broadbent** in **1931**. By plotting landmarks (such as **Sella**, **Nasion**, **Point A**, and **Point B**), the clinician derives angles that quantify the skeletal pattern. The most-used is the **ANB angle**, the difference between the SNA and SNB angles, which classifies the jaws: an ANB of about **2°** is skeletal Class I, a **larger** ANB indicates Class II, and a **negative or very small** ANB indicates Class III. Other systems include **Steiner's analysis**, **Downs' analysis**, and **Ricketts' analysis**. Cephalometrics turns a clinical impression of the face into reproducible numbers that guide whether a problem is dental or skeletal and whether growth modification, camouflage, or orthognathic surgery is required.

question.question: In Angle's classification, what defines a Class III (mesiocclusion) malocclusion?
options: The upper and lower first molars are in the ideal relationship.
The lower first molar is positioned distally (posteriorly) relative to the upper, giving an overbite profile.
The lower first molar is positioned mesially (anteriorly) relative to the upper, giving an underbite profile.
There is no contact between the upper and lower incisors.
question.explanation: Class III malocclusion is defined by the lower first molar sitting mesially (forward) of its ideal relationship to the upper first molar, producing a prognathic, "underbite" appearance. Option A describes Class I, option B describes Class II (overbite), and option D describes an open bite, which is a separate descriptor not part of Angle's molar classes.

hints: Class III is the protruding-lower-jaw, underbite pattern.
Think about whether the lower molar is forward (mesial) or back (distal).
slides.workedSolution: Angle's classification uses the relationship of the first permanent molars. In Class III (mesiocclusion), the lower first molar is displaced mesially — toward the front of the mouth — relative to the upper first molar, so the lower jaw and lower teeth sit ahead of the upper, producing the prognathic "underbite" profile. Class I is the normal molar relationship, and Class II is the opposite of Class III, with the lower molar distal to the upper and an overbite/retruded-chin profile.

question.question: Who discovered osseointegration, what material does it involve, and roughly when were the first titanium dental implants placed in a human?
question.explanation: Per-Ingvar Brånemark discovered that bone bonds directly to titanium (osseointegration) and placed the first titanium dental implants in a human, Gösta Larsson, in 1965. Angle (A) founded modern orthodontics; Buonocore (C) discovered acid-etching; Andrews (D) developed the straight-wire appliance — none of these relate to osseointegration.

hints: He was a Swedish orthopaedic surgeon studying bone with titanium chambers.
The metal is titanium and the year is in the 1960s.
slides.workedSolution: While studying bone healing using titanium optical chambers in the 1950s, the Swedish surgeon Per-Ingvar Brånemark found that bone fused so completely to titanium that the chamber could not be removed. He named this direct bone-to-metal bond osseointegration and applied it to tooth replacement, placing the first titanium dental implants in a patient named Gösta Larsson in 1965. This discovery is the foundation of modern implant dentistry; titanium remains the standard implant material because of its biocompatibility and reliable osseointegration.

question.question: In cephalometric analysis the ANB angle equals the SNA angle minus the SNB angle. If a patient has SNA = 84 degrees and SNB = 78 degrees, compute the ANB angle in degrees.
Why are flexible nickel–titanium (NiTi) archwires typically used in the early aligning stage of fixed orthodontic treatment?
options: Because they are the stiffest wires available and close spaces fastest.
Because their superelasticity delivers light, continuous forces that gently align crowded teeth.
Because they cannot be bonded to ceramic brackets.
Because they dissolve in saliva, requiring no removal.
question.explanation: NiTi wires are superelastic, so they spring back gently over a wide range of deflection, delivering light continuous forces ideal for the initial alignment of crowded, irregular teeth. They are flexible rather than the stiffest (option A — stiff stainless steel is used later), they work with all bracket types (C is false), and they do not dissolve (D).

hints: Think about which wire is most flexible and forgiving early on.
Light continuous force is the goal in initial alignment.
slides.workedSolution: Orthodontic treatment usually begins with flexible nickel–titanium archwires because their superelastic behaviour lets them be engaged into severely misaligned brackets yet deliver only light, continuous forces as they slowly return toward their original shape. Light continuous force is biologically optimal for tooth movement, recruiting osteoclasts and osteoblasts to remodel the alveolar bone without the hyalinisation and root resorption that heavy forces cause. As alignment improves, the clinician progresses to stiffer stainless-steel or beta-titanium wires for precise positioning, torque, and space closure.

question.question: An adult with a protruding upper jaw asks about braces versus clear aligners
question.prompt: A 30-year-old presents with crowded upper teeth, increased overjet, and a Class II Division 1 molar relationship; cephalometric analysis shows an ANB of 6 degrees. The patient wants the most discreet option and asks whether clear aligners (Invisalign) can fix the bite as well as fixed braces, and whether the protruding-jaw appearance can be corrected without surgery in an adult. Drawing on Angle's classification, cephalometric interpretation, the biomechanics of tooth movement, and the limits of growth modification in adults, explain what the ANB value indicates, how you would frame the aligner-versus-braces choice, and when surgery might be necessary.
